title: Fix a photo's lighting like a pro
goal: You will correct a photo’s overall exposure with Levels and Curves, refine local lighting with Dodge and Burn, and save a natural-looking edit.
prerequisites: A photo with exposure or lighting problems
Permission to save an edited copy of the photo

steps.action: Open the photo you want to correct.
steps.why: Opening the original photo creates the document you will edit.
steps.checkpoint: You should see the photo on the canvas and a Background layer in the Layers panel.
hint_levels: Start with the File menu at the top.
Choose Open, then locate the photo in the file browser.
Click File > Open, select the photo, and click Open.

steps.where: Layers panel on the right side of the workspace.
steps.why: A duplicate preserves the original pixels for comparison and recovery.
steps.checkpoint: You should see a new layer named Background copy above Background.
hint_levels: Look for the photo layer in the Layers panel.
The duplicate command is available by right-clicking the Background layer.
Right-click Background, click Duplicate Layer, and click OK.

steps.where: Bottom of the Layers panel > half-filled circle icon > Levels.
steps.why: Levels lets you set the darkest, brightest, and middle tones without changing the original pixels.
steps.checkpoint: You should see a Levels 1 layer and a histogram in the Properties panel.
hint_levels: Look along the bottom edge of the Layers panel.
Use the half-black, half-white circle called Create new fill or adjustment layer.
Click the half-filled circle icon, then click Levels.

steps.action: Move the black and white Input Levels sliders inward until each meets the visible edge of the histogram.
steps.where: Properties panel > Levels histogram > black left slider and white right slider.
steps.why: Aligning the endpoints restores useful contrast without unnecessarily clipping tones.
steps.checkpoint: The photo should have clearer contrast while retaining visible detail in bright and dark areas.
hint_levels: Watch the two outer sliders beneath the histogram.
Move each outer Input Levels slider only through the empty gap beside the histogram data.
Drag the black triangle from the left toward the histogram’s first data and the white triangle from the right toward its last data.

steps.action: Adjust the gray Input Levels slider slightly until the overall brightness looks balanced.
steps.where: Properties panel > Levels histogram > gray middle slider.
steps.why: The middle slider corrects midtone brightness without resetting the black and white endpoints.
steps.checkpoint: Faces or main subjects should look properly lit without highlights becoming blank or shadows becoming solid black.
hint_levels: Concentrate on the middle triangle beneath the histogram.
Move the gray slider left to brighten midtones or right to darken them.
Drag the middle Input Levels triangle in small movements, then stop when the subject looks naturally exposed.

steps.action: Add a Curves adjustment layer above the Levels layer.
steps.where: Bottom of the Layers panel > half-filled circle icon > Curves.
steps.why: Curves provides finer control over brightness and contrast after the basic Levels correction.
steps.checkpoint: You should see a Curves 1 layer above Levels 1 and a diagonal line in the Properties panel.
hint_levels: Return to the adjustment-layer control at the bottom of Layers.
Choose Curves from the Create new fill or adjustment layer menu.
Click the half-filled circle icon, then click Curves.

steps.action: Create a gentle S-shaped curve by raising one point in the brighter half and lowering one point in the darker half.
steps.where: Properties panel > Curves graph with the diagonal line.
steps.why: A subtle S-curve adds controlled contrast while keeping the lighting believable.
steps.checkpoint: The curve should resemble a shallow S and the photo should look slightly clearer rather than dramatically harsher.
hint_levels: Make two small changes on opposite halves of the diagonal line.
Lift the upper-right half slightly and lower the lower-left half slightly.
Click near the line’s upper-right quarter and drag slightly up, then click near its lower-left quarter and drag slightly down.

steps.action: Create a new 50% gray layer named Dodge and Burn using the Overlay blending mode.
steps.where: Menu bar > Layer > New > Layer dialog.
steps.why: An Overlay gray layer allows reversible local lightening and darkening without painting on the photo.
steps.checkpoint: You should see a transparent-looking Dodge and Burn layer above Curves 1 while the photo itself remains visible.
hint_levels: Use the New Layer dialog rather than the basic new-layer button.
The dialog includes Name, Mode, and a checkbox for filling with a neutral color.
Click Layer > New > Layer, enter Dodge and Burn, choose Overlay from Mode, check Fill with Overlay-neutral color (50% gray), and click OK.

steps.action: Select the Dodge Tool and set a soft brush with Exposure at 5%.
steps.where: Left Tools panel > Dodge Tool, then top Options bar > brush preset and Exposure.
steps.why: Low exposure and a soft edge build lightening gradually and reduce obvious retouching marks.
steps.checkpoint: The Dodge Tool is active, Exposure reads 5%, and the brush preview has a soft feathered edge.
hint_levels: Find the tool whose icon resembles a small lollipop.
It may share a tool slot with Burn Tool and Sponge Tool, and its settings appear across the top.
Click and hold the Dodge/Burn tool slot, choose Dodge Tool, choose a Soft Round brush in the Options bar, and set Exposure to 5%.

steps.action: Paint short strokes over only the shadow areas that need gentle brightening.
steps.where: Image canvas while the Dodge and Burn layer is selected in the Layers panel.
steps.why: Selective dodging reveals local detail without flattening all of the photo’s shadows.
steps.checkpoint: The chosen shadows should appear slightly lighter while nearby areas remain unchanged.
hint_levels: Work only where existing light should be strengthened.
Use several passes with a brush slightly larger than the area instead of one strong stroke.
Confirm Dodge and Burn is selected, resize the brush with the [ and ] keys, then click-drag short strokes over the shadows.

steps.action: Switch to the Burn Tool at 5% Exposure and paint over only the bright areas that need gentle darkening.
steps.where: Left Tools panel > Burn Tool, top Options bar > Exposure, then image canvas.
steps.why: Selective burning recovers visual balance and guides attention without making highlights look dirty.
steps.checkpoint: Distracting bright areas should look slightly darker while highlight texture remains visible.
hint_levels: Use the tool grouped with the Dodge Tool.
Keep Exposure low and build the effect in several passes.
Click and hold the Dodge Tool, choose Burn Tool, set Exposure to 5%, and paint short strokes over overly bright areas.

steps.action: Toggle the Dodge and Burn layer’s visibility to confirm the local correction is subtle, then save an editable PSD copy.
steps.where: Layers panel > eye icon beside Dodge and Burn, then menu bar > File > Save As.
steps.why: Comparing before and after catches excessive edits, and PSD preserves every adjustment layer.
steps.checkpoint: Turning the eye off and on shows a restrained lighting improvement, and a new .psd file appears in the chosen folder.
hint_levels: Compare the local edit before committing to the saved copy.
Use the layer’s eye icon for comparison, then save in Photoshop format under a new name.
Click the eye beside Dodge and Burn twice, reduce the layer Opacity if the change is strong, then click File > Save As, choose Photoshop (*.PSD), enter a new filename, and click Save.
